Listen to this article Share As political activities gather momentum ahead of the 2027 general elections, growing internal crises, leadership disagreements and factional divisions within Nigeria’s major political parties are raising questions about the future of the opposition. Observers are increasingly debating the possibility of a credible third political force challenging the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). ​While some political analysts believe the failure of opposition leaders to unite could strengthen the APC’s chances of securing another electoral victory, others argue that divisions within the ruling party itself could create opportunities for emerging political platforms, particularly the African Democratic Congress (ADC). ​Internal disagreements are normal in democracy ​Speaking exclusively with BusinessDay on whether the crises rocking opposition parties could destroy the third-force movement, Action Democratic Party National Publicity Secretary Sani Dawop dismissed suggestions that internal disagreements would necessarily lead to collapse. ​Dawop described disagreements as a normal feature of democratic organisations, arguing that political parties must develop effective mechanisms for managing differences rather than allowing them to threaten their existence. ​”Whatever any political gathering, association or group, there will always be differences, misunderstanding and conflict because there will be divergent opinions,” he said. ​Ruling party leverages state machinery ​He explained that even the ruling APC experiences internal disagreements and political crises but benefits from its control of government resources and established structures to manage dissent. ​”Even in the ruling party, there are differences and misunderstandings and internal crises, but because they are in government, they are using public resources to patronise people who have divergent views and opinions to go along the lines of those in control of the machinery of government,” Dawop alleged. ​He maintained that opposition parties were still consulting and had not concluded their political arrangements ahead of 2027. ​Opposition accuses ruling party of engineering crises ​Dawop also accused the ruling party of contributing to divisions within opposition parties, alleging that some of the crises were deliberately engineered to weaken alternative political platforms. ​”Most of these crises in the opposition are engineered by the ruling party,” he claimed. ​He further alleged that restrictions on opposition parties’ access to public spaces for political campaigns and publicity were part of efforts to limit their visibility. ​According to him, the opposition must strengthen its internal conflict-resolution mechanisms to prevent disagreements from escalating into damaging divisions. ​”We should therefore use our conflict-resolution mechanism to avert these differences through the reconciliation committee in the best interests against the ruling party,” he advised. ​Third-force prospects in Benue State ​Political analyst and university don Gberindyer Fidelis Aondover of the University of Agriculture, Makurdi, in an exclusive interview with BusinessDay, believes that the emerging political situation could favour the third force, particularly in Benue State. ​Aondover argued that the ADC has significant opportunities ahead of 2027 because of growing divisions within the APC and disagreements over political interests and candidate selection. ​”The third force has a very high chance of survival and victory because of the significant internal polarisation within the ruling political party (APC) and the existing clash of interests among candidates from the ruling party and the major opposition party,” he stated. ​Grassroots disaffection creates openings for ADC ​He cited the reported disaffection among members of the APC faction loyal to the Benue State governor following the replacement of their preferred National Assembly candidates with candidates associated with another faction believed to enjoy stronger support from the Presidency. ​According to him, the situation has created an opportunity for the ADC to attract aggrieved APC members and their supporters, particularly in constituencies where the displaced candidates enjoy considerable grassroots popularity. ​”Members of the governor’s faction and their followers who are angry about the replacement of their preferred National Assembly candidates may consider ADC as an alternative, especially where the replaced candidates are popular,” Aondover said. ​He, however, cautioned that the opportunity would not automatically translate into electoral victory. ​Electoral conversion requires strong organisation ​”Victory can only be assured if the party can convert this disaffection into votes and if its candidates are visible, credible and well organised,” he emphasised. ​Aondover predicted that the ADC could stand a strong chance of winning some National Assembly constituencies in Benue State, although its chances of capturing the governorship seat appeared less likely. ​”The most likely outcome is that the ADC, as the third force, has a very high chance of winning in some National Assembly constituencies but remains unlikely to win the governorship election in Benue State,” he said. ​He also identified potential opportunities for the ADC or the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the presidential contest, arguing that some supporters of the incumbent governor may become politically opposed to President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid because of their perception of the Presidency’s involvement in the APC’s internal divisions. ​Opposition disunity hands advantage to APC ​The concerns over opposition disunity have also attracted criticism from former Jigawa State governor Sule Lamido, who warned that the failure of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Labour Party’s 2023 presidential candidate, Peter Obi, to unite could hand the APC an easier victory in 2027. ​Lamido’s position highlights a major challenge confronting Nigeria’s opposition: the difficulty of building a common political front despite shared interests in challenging the ruling party. ​Beyond disagreements among the major opposition figures, internal leadership disputes within smaller political parties also raise questions about the strength and credibility of the proposed third force. ​Leadership crisis rocks Action Democratic Party ​One such example is the lingering crisis within the Action Democratic Party, where a faction has accused suspended National Chairman Yabagi Sani of attempting to alter the party’s constitution and registered identity without following due process. ​In a press statement dated November 13, 2026, and signed by Action Democratic Party National Secretary Victor Fingesi, the faction accused Sani of continuing to issue official correspondence in the party’s name despite his reported suspension. ​The statement alleged that Sani wrote to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), seeking recognition of a version of the ADP constitution which the faction claimed had not been validly adopted through the party’s prescribed constitutional procedures. ​Safeguarding constitutional integrity and party identity ​Fingesi cited Article 55 of the ADP Constitution, which stipulates procedures for constitutional amendments, including a two-thirds majority resolution, written consent from the Ethics and Values Council and subsequent approval at the National Convention. ​The statement stressed that these provisions were binding safeguards, declaring: “The Constitution must remain supreme. Party institutions must be respected. Decisions must emerge through legitimate processes, not unilateral declarations.” ​The faction also accused the former chairman of unilaterally redesigning the party’s registered logo by removing the hand holding an open book and replacing the original square design with a circle. ​It argued that such changes to the party’s identity could not be made without following the appropriate institutional and regulatory procedures. ​The statement further urged INEC to scrutinise the disputed constitutional document and reject any amendment that failed to meet the party’s constitutional and regulatory requirements. ​Calling for collective action to protect the party, Fingesi maintained that the ADP must not be personalised or subjected to the preferences of any individual. ​”This is bigger than any individual, faction or political ambition. It is about preserving the ADP as a credible democratic platform governed by rules, principles and respect for the rule of law,” the statement declared. ​It concluded with a strong reminder of collective ownership, stating: “The ADP belongs to its members, not to any individual. Its Constitution is binding on everyone without exception.” ​As the 2027 elections approach, the political equation remains uncertain. The APC could benefit from opposition disunity, but its own internal disagreements may create openings for emerging political platforms.
